subject: Mathematics
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 7 periods = 280 minutes
Total: 7 periods · 4h 40min

periods.activity_title: Naming the Unknown: From Situations to Expressions

textbook_items_in_class.description: Shabnam is 3 years older than Aftab. Derive the expression s = a + 3 for Shabnam's age from Aftab's; use it to find Shabnam's age when Aftab is 23.
Parthiv's L-shaped matchstick pattern: derive the expression 2n for the number of matchsticks needed to make n L-shapes.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 4.1 p.84
textbook_items_in_class.description: Write perimeter formulas for: (a) equilateral triangle; (b) regular pentagon; (c) regular hexagon.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 4.1 p.84
textbook_items_in_class.description: Write algebraic expressions for: (a) 5 more than a number; (b) 4 less than a number; (c) 2 less than 13 times a number; (d) 13 less than 2 times a number.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 4.1 p.84
homework.description: Munirathna joins a pipe of unknown length k metres to a 20 m pipe. Write the expression for the combined length.

time_bands.activity: Pose the question: Shabnam is always 3 years older than Aftab — what is her age when his is 10? 15? Any value a? Build a table together and read Example 1, section 4.1 p.81 (“Shabnam is 3 years older than Aftab. Derive the expression s = a + 3...”) to name what the class just created as a ‘letter-number’ and an ‘algebraic expression’.

Walk through Example 2, section 4.1 p.82 (“Parthiv’s L-shaped matchstick pattern: derive the expression 2n...”). Students draw 1, 2, 3 L-shapes with matchsticks (or tally on paper), record counts, and spot the doubling rule before the formula is written.

Students attempt Figure it Out Q1, section 4.1 p.84 (“Write perimeter formulas for: (a) equilateral triangle; (b) regular pentagon; (c) regular hexagon.”) individually, then compare with a partner. Establish the pattern: for a regular n-gon with side s the perimeter is n × s, linking the specific formulas to a common structure.

Figure it Out Q5, section 4.1 p.84 (“Write algebraic expressions for: (a) 5 more than a number; (b) 4 less...”). Students translate four English phrases into expressions and share, with the class correcting any reversal of subtraction order. Introduce Figure it Out Q2, section 4.1 p.84 as an extension task to complete outside class.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often confuse the direction of subtraction — '4 less than a number n' is n – 4, not 4 – n — so pause on Q5(b) and ask a student to read the phrase aloud before writing. The age-table in Example 1 is the key anchor: returning to it when students lose track of what the letter stands for reliably re-grounds understanding. For self-study, Example 4, section 4.1 p.83 shows the perimeter of a square as 4 × q and is a clean bridge to the polygon work students just did.
materials: Matchsticks or toothpicks (a handful per pair)

periods.activity_title: Expressions in Action: Cost, Calendar, and Arithmetic Rules

textbook_items_in_class.description: Ketaki’s coconut-jaggery cost: derive the two-variable expression c × 35 + j × 60 and use it to compute cost for 7 coconuts and 4 kg jaggery.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q7, section 4.1 p.85
textbook_items_in_class.description: In a 2 × 3 calendar grid with bottom-middle date ‘w’, write expressions for the dates in all blank cells.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 4.1 p.84
homework.description: Complete the table for total amount Krithika has given counts of ₹100, ₹20, and ₹5 notes, including the general algebraic expression 100x + 20y + 5z.

time_bands.activity: Work through Example 3, section 4.1 p.82 (“Ketaki’s coconut-jaggery cost: derive the two-variable expression c × 35 + j × 60...”). Students substitute concrete values first, then read the general expression. Emphasise that a two-variable expression is still evaluated by replacing each letter with a number.

Figure it Out Q7, section 4.1 p.85 (“In a 2 × 3 calendar grid with bottom-middle date ‘w’, write expressions for the dates in all blank cells.”). Students fill the grid using w as anchor, then verify by picking a real calendar week and checking all six cells match.

Introduce section 4.2 as a revision bridge: the same swapping, grouping and bracket rules that work with numbers will work with expressions when letters are replaced. Work through items 1, 2, and 5 from Figure it Out, section 4.2 p.85 (“23 – 10 × 2; 83 + 28 – 13 + 32; 68 – (18 + 13)...”) together, naming each rule (operator precedence, commutativity, distribute-the-negative) as it appears.

Students complete items 3, 4, 6, 7 from Figure it Out, section 4.2 p.85 independently. Pairs swap papers and check; any item where both partners get different answers is placed on the board for class discussion.

periods.teacher_notes: A common error in the calendar-grid task is treating subtraction from w as addition — remind students that the date to the left of w is w – 1 and the date one row up is w – 7. Watch for students who expand 68 – (18 + 13) as 68 – 18 + 13 instead of 68 – 18 – 13; this misconception about distributing the negative carries directly into algebraic bracket removal in section 4.4.
materials: A printed or drawn 2×3 calendar grid (one per pair)

textbook_segments.title: Omission of the Multiplication Symbol in Algebraic Expressions

periods.activity_title: Reading the Shorthand: What Does 4n Really Mean?

textbook_items_in_class.description: Mind the Mistake, Mend the Mistake: nine algebraic substitutions (e.g. if a = –4, then 10 – a = 6; if d = 6, then 3d = 36; etc.). For each: identify whether there is a mistake, explain what went wrong, and give the correct value.

time_bands.activity: Write on the board: 4, 8, 12, 16, … Ask students what the nth term is. After a quick show of hands, reveal that the pattern is 4n, then unpack the notation: 4n means 4 × n, numbers are written before letters, and the multiplication symbol is omitted. Evaluate 7k when k = 4 and 5m + 3 when m = 2 together so the substitution process is explicit.

Present Figure it Out, section 4.3 p.87 (“Mind the Mistake, Mend the Mistake: nine algebraic substitutions...”). Students work in pairs on items 1–5, deciding for each: is there a mistake? What rule was broken? What is the correct value? Circulate and listen for the two key confusions: treating 10 – a as 10 – |–a| and reading 3d as the two-digit number 36.

Pairs report on items 1–5; class votes on whether each is correct or erroneous before the reporter reveals the answer. Complete items 6–9 in the same format, now working individually. Focus discussion on item involving concatenation confusion (3d = 36 when d = 6) — write 3d = 3 × d beside 36 (a two-digit number) to make the distinction visible.

Close with a rapid oral round: teacher says an expression and a value, students call out the result. Use examples that revisit all three error types surfaced in the exercise — sign errors in subtraction, concatenation, and correct evaluation — to consolidate the correct interpretation of the shorthand.

periods.teacher_notes: The concatenation error (3d = 36 when d = 6) is the most persistent misconception in this section; writing 3d = 3 × d visibly and asking 'would 3 × 6 give 36?' is the most direct correction. Also watch for sign errors when substituting negative values: 10 – a with a = –4 becomes 10 – (–4) = 14, not 6, and students who skip the bracket around the negative value consistently get this wrong.

periods.activity_title: Why Like Terms Combine: An Area-Based Argument

textbook_items_in_class.description: Big rectangle split into two smaller rectangles: show 4v + 3v = 7v and 12n – 4n = 8n using two methods of computing area.
Chair-table rental shop: simplify (40x + 75y) – (6x + 10y) to 34x + 65y by distributing the negative sign and collecting like terms.
Show that 5u and 5 + u are not equal by evaluating both for u = 2, 5, 8; similarly compare 10y – 3 and 10(y – 3) for several values of y.

time_bands.activity: Begin with the rectangle perimeter derivation: a rectangle of length l and breadth b has perimeter l + b + l + b. Ask: can this be written more compactly? Establish 2l + 2b as the simplified form. Then open Example 6, section 4.4 p.89 (“Big rectangle split into two smaller rectangles: show 4v + 3v = 7v and 12n – 4n = 8n using two methods of computing area.”). Students draw the split rectangle themselves and verify that both area routes give the same result — this is the deductive justification for why like terms combine.

Define like terms (same letter part, possibly different coefficient) and unlike terms. Walk through Example 7, section 4.4 p.90 (“Chair-table rental shop: simplify (40x + 75y) – (6x + 10y) to 34x + 65y...”). Emphasise the two-step logic: distribute the negative sign first, then collect x-terms and y-terms separately. Ask students to predict what happens if the sign is not distributed before collecting.

Example 10, section 4.4 p.92 (“Show that 5u and 5 + u are not equal by evaluating both for u = 2, 5, 8...”). Students build a two-column table substituting three values and confirm the expressions diverge. Extend: ask why 5u ≠ 5 + u in general — students reason from the table to the algebraic argument.

Quick pair-discussion: when are two algebraic expressions equal? Students articulate that equality holds for all substitutions, not just one — securing the definition of equivalent expressions before the next practice unit.

periods.teacher_notes: The rectangle-split diagram in Example 6 is the chapter’s clearest visual proof that like terms combine; insist that students draw it rather than just watch. The most common error in Example 7 is subtracting only the first term inside the bracket — write the full distribution step (–(6x + 10y) = –6x – 10y) explicitly before collecting. Example 9, section 4.4 p.92 (distributive expansion of 4(x + y) – y) is a useful self-study worked example for students who want a further bracket-removal challenge.
materials: Squared paper or plain paper for rectangle diagrams

periods.activity_title: Simplifying Confidently: Grids, Steps, and Mistake-Mending

textbook_items_in_class.description: Pencil-eraser shop over three days: simplify 5c + 3c + 10c = 18c using the distributive property; set up 18c + 11d for total earnings.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 4.4 p.93
textbook_items_in_class.description: Add the numbers in each of three grid pictures (containing letter-number terms like 5y, x, –6, 2p, 3q, –5g, 5k, etc.). Write corresponding expressions and simplify; try at least two different grouping methods and confirm the same result.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 4.4 p.94
textbook_items_in_class.description: Simplify each expression: (a) p+p+p+p; p+p+p+q; p+q+p–q; (b) p–q+p–q; p+q–p+q; (c) p+q–(p+q); p–q–p–q; (d) 2d–d–d–d; 2d–d–d–c; (e) 2d–d–(d–c); 2d–(d–d)–c; (f) 2d–d–c–c.

Mind the Mistake, Mend the Mistake: eleven algebraic simplifications (e.g. 3a+2b = 5; 6(p+2) = 6p+8; 5–(2–6z) = 3–6z; etc.). For each: identify the mistake, explain it, and give the correct simplest form.

time_bands.activity: Revisit the distributive property in action through Example 5, section 4.4 p.88 (“Pencil-eraser shop over three days: simplify 5c + 3c + 10c = 18c using the distributive property...”). Frame it as: the shop sold erasers on three days — how do we find the total in one expression? Students follow the grouping, then set up 18c + 11d independently.

Figure it Out Q1, section 4.4 p.93 (“Add the numbers in each of three grid pictures...”). Students work individually on grid 1, then in pairs on grids 2 and 3, each time using two different grouping sequences and confirming the same simplified answer. This concretely demonstrates commutativity for algebraic addition.

Figure it Out Q2, section 4.4 p.94 (“Simplify each expression: (a) p+p+p+p; p+p+p+q...”). Students work through the fifteen sub-parts in order. The sub-parts form a deliberate escalation — from pure addition to mixed signs to nested brackets — so students should not skip ahead.

Figure it Out, section 4.4 p.94 (“Mind the Mistake, Mend the Mistake: eleven algebraic simplifications...”). Work items 1–4 together, asking a student to name the rule being violated before the correction is written. Students finish the remaining items independently, then exchange notebooks for a partner check.

periods.teacher_notes: The grid exercise builds the crucial habit of re-checking by grouping differently; insist that students write both groupings rather than just stating the answer is the same. In the Mistake-Mending exercise, the error 3a + 2b = 5 (treating unlike terms as like) and 6(p + 2) = 6p + 8 (distributing to only the first term) are the two that recur most in student work — give these extra board time. Example 8, section 4.4 p.91 (Charu’s quiz scores) makes a useful self-study extension for students who finish early.

periods.activity_title: Formula Detective: Reverse-Engineering Rules from Patterns

textbook_items_in_class.description: Saree-border repeating pattern A, B, C, D, E, F: derive that design C appears at position 3n, design B at 3n – 1, design A at 3n – 2; use remainder on division by 3 to identify designs at positions 99, 122, 148.

Formula Detective: find the formulas for two number machines shown (input-output diagrams with 4–5 pairs each) and write the algebraic expression for each set of inputs, including the general a, b expression.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q11, section 4.5 p.103
textbook_items_in_class.description: Rope-cutting pattern: 1 cut → 2 pieces; fold once + cut → 3 pieces. Observe the pattern and find: (a) pieces if folded 10 times and cut; (b) expression for pieces when folded r times and cut.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q13, section 4.5 p.104
homework.description: Traffic signal colour sequence (R, G, Y, R, G, Y, …): find the colour at positions 90, 190, and 343; write expressions for positions of each colour.

time_bands.activity: Work through Example 12, section 4.5 p.96 (“Saree-border repeating pattern A, B, C, D, E, F: derive that design C appears at position 3n...”). Students list the first twelve positions and mark which design occupies each, then discover the 3n / 3n–1 / 3n–2 structure. The remainder-on-division-by-3 argument is then articulated together: position 99 ÷ 3 leaves remainder 0, so remainder 0 means the last design in the triplet.

Figure it Out, section 4.5 p.95 (“Formula Detective: find the formulas for two number machines...”). Students study each input-output table, hypothesise a rule, test it on a second pair, revise if needed, and write the general algebraic expression. Pairs explain their reasoning to another pair before sharing with the class.

Figure it Out Q11, section 4.5 p.103 (“Rope-cutting pattern: 1 cut → 2 pieces; fold once + cut → 3 pieces...”). Students act out the first three cases by folding a strip of paper, record the results, identify the linear pattern, and write the expression for r folds. Connect this to the saree-border method: spotting a per-step increment and encoding it as a coefficient. Assign Figure it Out Q13, section 4.5 p.104 for independent practice outside class.

periods.teacher_notes: Students sometimes confuse the remainder of 0 (position is a multiple of 3, so it is design C) with 'no remainder means the pattern restarts at A' — work through position 6 explicitly to anchor this. In the Formula Detective task, some pairs guess a formula that works for the first pair but fails the second; normalise revision as part of the mathematical process rather than treating the first guess as wrong. The calendar 2×2 diagonal proof (always 2a + 8) in section 4.5 is a strong self-study reading for students who want to see algebraic modelling used as a proof.
materials: Strips of paper (one per student, for the rope-cutting task)

periods.activity_title: Expressions at Work: Situations, Paths, and Growing Patterns

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 4.5 p.102
textbook_items_in_class.description: One plate of Jowar roti costs ₹30 and pulao costs ₹20. Which of the expressions (a)–(e) correctly describes the total amount earned for x rotis and y pulaos?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 4.5 p.102
textbook_items_in_class.description: Snail in a well: climbs u cm by day, slips d cm by night for 10 days/nights. (a) Write the expression for net distance from start. (b) What can we say if d > u?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q12, section 4.5 p.104
textbook_items_in_class.description: Matchstick square pattern: identify the pattern, find how many matchsticks for 10 squares, and write the expression for w squares.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q7, section 4.5 p.103

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q14, section 4.5 p.104
homework.description: Step-sequence growing square pattern: how many squares in Step 4, Step 10, Step 50? Write a general formula. How does the formula change if counting vertices instead of squares?

time_bands.activity: Figure it Out Q1, section 4.5 p.102 (“One plate of Jowar roti costs ₹30 and pulao costs ₹20. Which of the expressions (a)–(e) correctly describes the total amount earned...”). Students eliminate wrong options by substituting x = 2, y = 3 and checking which expression gives the expected ₹100. Bridge explicitly to the two-variable cost formula from section 4.1 (coconut-jaggery) — same structure, new context.

Figure it Out Q3, section 4.5 p.102 (“Snail in a well: climbs u cm by day, slips d cm by night for 10 days/nights...”). Students write the net change per day (u – d) and scale it to 10 cycles: 10(u – d). Part (b) requires reasoning: if d > u, the expression is negative, meaning the snail moves backward overall. Students write a sentence justifying this from the expression.

Figure it Out Q12, section 4.5 p.104 (“Matchstick square pattern: identify the pattern, find how many matchsticks for 10 squares, and write the expression for w squares.”). Students draw steps 1, 2, 3 and count matchsticks, then identify the per-square increment and derive the expression. Compare the formula structure with the L-shape formula from section 4.1 — both have the form an + b.

Figure it Out Q7, section 4.5 p.103 (“Simplify: (a) 3a+9b–6+8a–4b–7a+16...”). Students tackle all six sub-parts, which integrate multi-variable collection, bracket removal, and the distributive property developed across sections 4.3 and 4.4. Assign Figure it Out Q14, section 4.5 p.104 as an extension task for independent completion.

periods.teacher_notes: The snail problem is the unit’s best reasoning checkpoint: a student who can write 10(u – d) and interpret the sign of the result has genuinely linked expression-writing to contextual meaning. In the matchstick square pattern, watch for students who count all sides of each square separately and reach 4w — prompt them to look at how many new sticks each additional square needs, not the total sticks in all squares. The simplification problems in Q7 reward students who have consolidated bracket removal from section 4.4; any student struggling there benefits from revisiting Example 7, section 4.4 p.90.
materials: Matchsticks or toothpicks (optional, for pattern drawing)

items.prompt: Which of the following correctly describes what the letter-number n represents in the algebraic expression 2n?

options.label: A
options.text: A fixed value that is always equal to 2

options.label: B
options.text: A quantity that can take different numerical values, and 2n means 2 multiplied by n

options.label: C
options.text: The digit placed next to 2 to form the two-digit number 2n

options.label: D
options.text: The number of times we add 2, but n itself has no separate value

teacher_guide.expected_answer: B — A letter-number (variable) can take different numerical values; 2n means 2 multiplied by n, not a two-digit number and not a fixed constant.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Recall the definition of a letter-number and the shorthand multiplication convention introduced in section 4.1.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student treats the letter-number as a constant rather than a variable quantity.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student confuses algebraic notation with place-value concatenation, the key misconception flagged in section 4.3.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student conflates repeated addition with counting and does not recognise n as an independent quantity.

inclusivity.support: Allow the student to look back at the age table in Example 1, section 4.1 and substitute a few values for n.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to write their own real-world situation where n is a letter-number and 2n describes a total.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 4.1 p.84
exercise.description: Write perimeter formulas for: (a) equilateral triangle; (b) regular pentagon; (c) regular hexagon.

items.section_title: Omission of the Multiplication Symbol in Algebraic Expressions
items.prompt: A student wrote: "If k = 5, then 3k = 35." Which statement best identifies the error?

options.label: A
options.text: The student should have added 3 and 5 to get 8, not written 35.

options.label: B
options.text: The student confused the shorthand 3k with the two-digit number formed by placing 3 and 5 side by side, instead of computing 3 × 5 = 15.

options.label: C
options.text: The student subtracted incorrectly; 3k means k – 3, so the answer should be 2.

options.label: D
options.text: There is no error; 3k = 35 when k = 5 is correct.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: B — The notation 3k means 3 × k. When k = 5, the value is 3 × 5 = 15, not the two-digit number 35 formed by writing the digits together.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the multiplication-shorthand convention from section 4.3: 3k = 3 × k, so substitute and multiply.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student believes the shorthand means addition, misreading 3k as 3 + k.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student misinterprets the coefficient as a subtrahend rather than a multiplier.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has not recognised the concatenation error at all, accepting the two-digit misread.

inclusivity.support: Encourage the student to write 3k as 3 × k explicitly before substituting any value.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to create a second example of the same concatenation error using a different expression and value, then correct it.

exercise.description: Mind the Mistake, Mend the Mistake: nine algebraic substitutions (e.g. if a = –4, then 10 – a = 6; if d = 6, then 3d = 36; etc.). For each: identify whether there is a mistake, explain what went wrong, and give the correct value.

items.prompt: A rectangle has length l and breadth b. Priya writes its perimeter as l + b + l + b and then simplifies to 2l + 2b. Rohan says 2l + 2b and 2(l + b) are two different expressions. Explain whether Rohan is correct or incorrect, using at least one substitution to support your reasoning.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Rohan is incorrect. 2(l + b) = 2l + 2b by the distributive property, so the two expressions are equivalent — they give the same value for every pair of values of l and b. For example, with l = 5 and b = 3: 2l + 2b = 10 + 6 = 16, and 2(l + b) = 2 × 8 = 16. Two algebraic expressions are equal when they yield identical values for all substitutions, and this pair does.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the distributive property (section 4.4) to expand 2(l + b) and confirm it equals 2l + 2b for all values.

inclusivity.support: Pair the student with a partner to talk through the substitution aloud before writing.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to alter the perimeter formula to 3l + 2b and decide whether a factored form like 2(l + b) + l is equivalent, justifying with two substitutions.

exercise.description: Big rectangle split into two smaller rectangles: show 4v + 3v = 7v and 12n – 4n = 8n using two methods of computing area.

items.prompt: A repeating colour sequence goes: Red, Blue, Green, Red, Blue, Green, … continuing forever. Arnav claims that the colour at any position that is a multiple of 3 is always Green, and the colour at any position one less than a multiple of 3 is always Blue. Justify Arnav's claim by writing algebraic expressions for the positions of each colour and explaining how the remainder on division by 3 determines the colour.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The pattern repeats every 3 positions: position 1 = Red, 2 = Blue, 3 = Green, 4 = Red, 5 = Blue, 6 = Green, and so on. Positions of Green are 3, 6, 9, … which are the multiples of 3, written as 3n (n = 1, 2, 3, …). Positions of Blue are 2, 5, 8, … which are one less than multiples of 3, written as 3n – 1. Positions of Red are 1, 4, 7, … written as 3n – 2. To find the colour at any position p, divide p by 3: if the remainder is 0 then it is Green (p is a multiple of 3); if the remainder is 2 then it is Blue (p = 3n – 1); if the remainder is 1 then it is Red (p = 3n – 2). Arnav's claim is correct.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Express positions of each colour as 3n, 3n – 1, 3n – 2 and use the remainder on division by 3 to classify any given position, following the method of section 4.5.

inclusivity.support: Suggest the student list the first nine positions in a table and identify which colour sits at each before writing the expression.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to modify the argument for a 4-colour repeating sequence and write the four position expressions.

exercise.description: Saree-border repeating pattern A, B, C, D, E, F: derive that design C appears at position 3n, design B at 3n – 1, design A at 3n – 2; use remainder on division by 3 to identify designs at positions 99, 122, 148.

items.prompt: A school canteen sells samosas for ₹8 each and juice bottles for ₹15 each. Write an algebraic expression for the total amount earned when s samosas and j juice bottles are sold. Use your expression to find the total when 12 samosas and 5 juice bottles are sold.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The expression is 8s + 15j. When s = 12 and j = 5: 8 × 12 + 15 × 5 = 96 + 75 = ₹171.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Form a two-variable cost expression (unit price × quantity for each item, then add) and substitute the given values, following the method of section 4.1.

inclusivity.support: Encourage the student to draw a small table with s = 1, 2, 3 and compute the samosa cost alone before adding the juice term.
inclusivity.challenge: Change one number: the canteen offers a ₹5 discount when the combined bill exceeds ₹150 — modify the expression and find the final amount for the same quantities.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 4.1 p.84
exercise.description: Write algebraic expressions for: (a) 5 more than a number; (b) 4 less than a number; (c) 2 less than 13 times a number; (d) 13 less than 2 times a number.

items.prompt: Evaluate the expression 45 – (12 + 8) + 6 × 3 using the correct order of operations. Show each step clearly.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Step 1 — Brackets: 12 + 8 = 20. Step 2 — Multiplication: 6 × 3 = 18. Step 3 — Left to right: 45 – 20 + 18 = 25 + 18 = 43.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the order of operations from section 4.2: evaluate brackets first, then multiplication, then addition and subtraction left to right.

inclusivity.support: Provide a number line or a blank step-by-step template labelled Brackets → Multiplication → Addition/Subtraction.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to insert a pair of brackets somewhere else in the expression that changes the final answer, then evaluate that new expression.

items.prompt: A sports shop charges ₹50x + ₹90y for renting x badminton rackets and y cricket bats per day. The shop owner deducts a maintenance fee of ₹(8x + 12y) from the day's earnings. Write and simplify an expression for the net earnings. Then find the net earnings when x = 6 and y = 4.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Net earnings = (50x + 90y) – (8x + 12y). Distribute the negative: 50x + 90y – 8x – 12y. Collect like terms: (50 – 8)x + (90 – 12)y = 42x + 78y. When x = 6 and y = 4: 42 × 6 + 78 × 4 = 252 + 312 = ₹564.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Distribute the negative sign across the bracket, collect like terms (section 4.4), then substitute the given values.

inclusivity.support: Suggest the student use an alternate representation: draw two columns labelled 'racket terms' and 'bat terms' to sort like terms before combining.
inclusivity.challenge: Change the constraint: the maintenance fee is now ₹(8x + 12y + 20) — modify the simplified expression and recompute the net earnings for x = 6, y = 4.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 4.4 p.93
exercise.description: Add the numbers in each of three grid pictures (containing letter-number terms like 5y, x, –6, 2p, 3q, –5g, 5k, etc.). Write corresponding expressions and simplify; try at least two different grouping methods and confirm the same result.

items.prompt: Matchstick hexagons are built in a row: the first hexagon uses 6 matchsticks, each additional hexagon shares one side with the previous one and adds 5 new matchsticks. Write an algebraic expression for the total number of matchsticks needed to build h hexagons in a row. Use your expression to find the number of matchsticks for 8 hexagons.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The first hexagon uses 6 matchsticks. Each subsequent hexagon adds 5. For h hexagons: total = 6 + 5(h – 1) = 6 + 5h – 5 = 5h + 1. For h = 8: 5 × 8 + 1 = 41 matchsticks.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Identify the starting value and per-step increment, form a linear expression of the type an + b (section 4.5), then substitute h = 8.

inclusivity.support: Encourage the student to draw the first three hexagon chains and count matchsticks, recording results in a table before writing the expression.
inclusivity.challenge: Modify the parameter: each additional hexagon now shares two sides with the chain instead of one — re-derive the expression for h hexagons.
